content: Secondary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menstrual periods for six or more consecutive months in a woman who previously had regular menstrual cycles. Amenorrhea, in general, refers to the absence of a woman’s monthly menstrual cycle or period. Symptoms of Secondary Amenorrhea: The primary symptom is the absence of menstrual periods for six months or longer. The individual must have previously experienced one or more spontaneous menstrual cycles. Additional symptoms that may accompany secondary amenorrhea include: Changes in breast size. Significant weight gain or weight loss. Discharge from the breasts, known as galactorrhea. Headaches. Increased hair growth in a male-pattern distribution (hirsutism) and acne. Vaginal dryness. Changes in voice pitch or tone. If secondary amenorrhea is caused by a pituitary tumor, symptoms such as vision loss may also occur. Causes of Secondary Amenorrhea: Women who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or in menopause are not classified as having secondary amenorrhea. Women using hormonal contraceptives, such as birth control pills or Depo-Provera injections, may experience an absence of monthly bleeding. After discontinuing these hormones, it may take more than six months for menstrual cycles to resume. Risk factors for secondary amenorrhea include: Obesity. Excessive and prolonged physical exercise. Having less than 15–17% body fat. Severe anxiety or emotional distress. Sudden and significant weight loss, such as from a strict diet or gastric bypass surgery. Other potential causes include: Pituitary tumors in the brain. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Premature ovarian failure. Thyroid dysfunction. Certain medications may also lead to missed periods, including: Busulfan. Chemotherapy drugs for cancer. Chlorambucil. Cyclophosphamide. Phenothiazines. High-Risk Factors: Procedures such as dilation and curettage (D&C) can result in the formation of scar tissue, leading to a condition called Asherman syndrome, which may cause cessation of menstruation. Severe pelvic infections can also lead to scarring and secondary amenorrhea. When to Seek Medical Attention: It is important to schedule an appointment with a primary care provider or OB/GYN if you have missed more than one menstrual period. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential. Diagnosis: A physical examination and pelvic exam are necessary to rule out pregnancy, and a pregnancy test will be conducted. Blood tests may be performed to evaluate hormone levels, including: Estradiol. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Luteinizing hormone (LH). Prolactin. Testosterone. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). Additional diagnostic tests may include: CT scan of the head. Endometrial biopsy. Genetic testing. MRI of the head. Pelvic ultrasound or hysterosonogram. Treatment Options: Treatment depends on the underlying cause of the amenorrhea. Once the primary condition is addressed, normal menstrual cycles typically resume. For example: If hypothyroidism is the cause, treatment with thyroid supplements will resolve the amenorrhea. If obesity, excessive exercise, or weight loss is the cause, treatment may involve modifying exercise routines or implementing weight control measures. Prognosis: The outlook for secondary amenorrhea depends on its cause. Most conditions that lead to secondary amenorrhea respond well to treatment. Possible Complications: Complications vary depending on the underlying cause of the amenorrhea. While amenorrhea itself may be harmless, it can sometimes be associated with overgrowth of the uterine lining (endometrial hyperplasia), which may increase the risk of uterine cancer. Other complications may arise depending on the specific cause of the amenorrhea.
